'''Frederic Mather Lord''' (November 12, 1912 – February 5, 2000) was a [[psychometrics|psychometrician]] for [[Educational Testing Service]]. The [[SAT]], [[Graduate Record Examinations|GRE]], [[GMAT]], [[LSAT]] and [[TOEFL]] are all based on Lord's research.

==Early life==
Lord was born on November 12, 1912, in Hanover, New Hampshire. His great-great-grandfather, [[Nathan Lord]], served as the sixth president of [[Dartmouth College]], from which Lord graduated with a bachelor's degree in Sociology in 1936.<ref name="nytimesobit">{{cite news |last1=Steinberg |first1=Jacques |title=Frederic Lord, Who Devised Testing Yardstick, Dies at 87 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/02/10/us/frederic-lord-who-devised-testing-yardstick-dies-at-87.html |accessdate=October 26, 2018 |work=The New York Times |date=February 10, 2000}}</ref> He later earned a master's degree in Educational Psychology from the [[University of Minnesota]], followed by a PhD in Psychology from [[Princeton University]] in 1951.<ref name="nytimesobit"/><ref name="latimesobit">{{cite news |title=Frederick Lord; Pioneer In Testing |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/161637910/?terms=%22Frederic%2BLord%22 |accessdate=October 26, 2018 |work=The Los Angeles Times |date=February 16, 2000|page=A22|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|url-access=registration }}</ref>

==Career==
Lord first worked for the [[Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching|Carnegie Foundation]] in 1944.<ref name="nytimesobit"/><ref name="latimesobit"/> By 1950, he began working for the [[Educational Testing Service]] (ETS).<ref name="latimesobit"/> He was the source of much of the seminal research on [[item response theory]],<ref>[http://www.ets.org/portal/site/ets/menuitem.c988ba0e5dd572bada20bc47c3921509/?vgnextoid=26fdaf5e44df4010VgnVCM10000022f95190RCRD&vgnextchannel=ceb2be3a864f4010VgnVCM10000022f95190RCRD ETS Research Overview]</ref> including two important books: ''Statistical Theories of Mental Test Scores'' (1968, with [[Melvin R. Novick]], and two chapters by [[Allan Birnbaum]]), and ''Applications of Item Response Theory to Practical Testing Problems'' (1980).

Lord's research shaped the [[SAT]], [[Graduate Record Examinations|GRE]], [[GMAT]], [[LSAT]] and the [[TOEFL]].<ref name="nytimesobit"/><ref name="latimesobit"/> Lord was called the "Father of Modern Testing" by the [[National Council on Measurement in Education]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ncme.org/news/newsdetail.cfm?ID=21&ArchView=y |title=NCME News: Frederic Lord, Father of Modern Testing, Dies at 87 |access-date=2008-02-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060821214202/http://www.ncme.org/news/newsdetail.cfm?ID=21&ArchView=y |archive-date=2006-08-21 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
Lord was married twice. He had three sons with his first wife. His second wife was Muriel Kendall.<ref name="nytimesobit"/>

Lord died on February 5, 2000, in [[Naples, Florida]], at 87.<ref name="nytimesobit"/><ref name="latimesobit"/>
